# Lab: a managed node waits for its cue

<!-- type: tutorial · level: 2 · topic: lifecycle -->

**Needs first:** [Parameters and launch files](parameters-and-launch-files.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: chapter status -->
> **Status:** this chapter runs on [`nros-board-mps2-an385-freertos`](../reference/board-support-levels.md#mps2-an385-freertos): Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry; [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.

Most nodes start work the moment their image boots. Some should not: a
motor controller that must wait until its supervisor has checked the
system, a sensor that must not publish until it is calibrated, a node a
test wants to start at a known moment. ROS 2 gives such a node a lifecycle
(REP-2002): a small state machine that something outside the node drives,
and that decides when the node may do its work. A node with one is called a
managed node.

nano-ros runs the same state machine, under the node's own name, with the
same five services and the same `ros2 lifecycle` commands as stock ROS 2. In
this lab you make the talker of the Tutorial a managed node, boot it, and
watch it stay silent until you activate it from the host. You then switch
it off again, try a transition the state machine refuses, and finally let
it boot straight to work.

At the end, `ros2 lifecycle get /sensor_node` answers `active [3]` and the
listener prints `I heard:` again, but only after you said so.

The lab starts from the workspace of chapter 7, *Parameters and launch
files*: `sensor_node` publishes on `/sensor/reading` every 500 ms, and
`monitor_node` listens. Run every step from the root of `sensor_ws`, in a
shell where ROS 2 is sourced. It takes about half an hour, most of it
reading. Nothing in it changes your nodes' code: the lifecycle is a fact of
the system, written in the launch file and in `system.toml`.

## The four states

A managed node is always in one of four primary states:

| State | What the node does | How it gets there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `unconfigured` | Exists, but holds nothing it needs to work | Boot, or `cleanup` from `inactive` |
| `inactive` | Configured: it could work, but does not | `configure` from `unconfigured`, or `deactivate` from `active` |
| `active` | Works | `activate` from `inactive` |
| `finalized` | Done; it never leaves | `shutdown` from any of the three above |

The words in the last column are transitions. Something outside the node
asks for one, the node runs the matching step (in this lab, a default step
that always succeeds), and the machine moves on. A transition that does not
start from the node's current state is refused.

What "works" means is the part nano-ros enforces for you: a managed node's
publishers send only while the node is `active`. In every other state,
`publish` returns success and the message is dropped. Its subscriptions,
timers, services and its log are not gated: they work in every state, so
the node can keep listening while it waits.

## Mark the talker managed

A node is managed when the system says so. Change the talker's `<node>` in
the launch file to `<lifecycle_node>`. The tree marks the two files this lab
changes with `*`:

```tree
sensor_ws/
  src/
    sensor_node_bringup/
      launch/
        system.launch.xml   *
      system.toml           *
```

```xml probe=2410 track=installed variant=qemu file=src/sensor_node_bringup/launch/system.launch.xml
<?xml version="1.0"?>
<launch>
  <arg name="topic" default="/sensor/reading"/>

  <lifecycle_node pkg="sensor_node" exec="sensor_node" name="sensor_node">
    <param name="period_ms" value="500"/>
    <remap from="/reading" to="$(var topic)"/>
  </lifecycle_node>
  <node pkg="monitor_node" exec="monitor_node" name="monitor_node">
    <remap from="/reading" to="$(var topic)"/>
  </node>
  <node pkg="server_node" exec="server_node" name="server_node"/>
  <node pkg="client_node" exec="client_node" name="client_node"/>
  <node pkg="action_server_node" exec="action_server_node" name="action_server_node"/>
  <node pkg="action_client_node" exec="action_client_node" name="action_client_node"/>
</launch>
```

Only the talker's element changed. `monitor_node` stays a plain node: it
has no state machine and listens from boot, as an `rclcpp::Node` would.

By default a managed node is brought to `active` as the image boots, so
nothing would look different. Tell the image to leave it where it starts.
Add this to the end of the bringup's `system.toml`:

```toml probe=2420 track=installed variant=qemu append=src/sensor_node_bringup/system.toml

[lifecycle]
autostart = "none"
```

`autostart` names the state every managed node of the image boots to:
`"none"` leaves them `unconfigured`, `"inactive"` configures them, and
`"active"` (the default) configures and activates them.

## Boot it, and watch nothing happen

```bash probe=2430 probe-run=900 probe-keep track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run
```

```text probe-expect=2430 variant=qemu
Publishing every 500 ms
while its node is not active
```

The talker's timer still fires every 500 ms: timers are not gated. But its
first publish prints one line, and every message after it is dropped:

```text
publishing on `/sensor/reading` while its node is not active: the message is dropped, and so is every message until the node is activated
```

The listener prints nothing, because nothing reaches it. Leave `nros run`
running, and open a second shell in `sensor_ws` for the rest of the lab.

## Ask the node where it is

```bash probe=2440 probe-run=120 probe-exit=0 track=installed variant=qemu
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 lifecycle nodes --no-daemon --spin-time 3
ros2 lifecycle get /sensor_node --no-daemon --spin-time 3
```

```text probe-expect=2440 variant=qemu
/sensor_node
unconfigured [1]
```

`--no-daemon --spin-time 3` asks the board directly, giving discovery
three seconds, as chapter 7 did for `ros2 topic list`.

`ros2 lifecycle nodes` lists exactly the image's managed nodes: the talker,
under its own name. The listener and the service and action nodes are not
there, because they have no state machine. The number after each state is
its REP-2002 id.

Each managed node answers five services under its own name:
`/sensor_node/get_state`, `/sensor_node/change_state`,
`/sensor_node/get_available_states`, `/sensor_node/get_available_transitions`
and `/sensor_node/get_transition_graph`. The `ros2 lifecycle` verbs call
them; a supervisor node of your own can call them too.

## Configure it

```bash probe=2450 probe-run=120 probe-exit=0 track=installed variant=qemu
ros2 lifecycle set /sensor_node configure --no-daemon --spin-time 3
ros2 lifecycle get /sensor_node --no-daemon --spin-time 3
```

```text probe-expect=2450 variant=qemu
Transitioning successful
inactive [2]
```

The node is configured, and still silent: `inactive` is not `active`. The
listener's console still prints nothing.

## Activate it

```bash probe=2460 probe-run=120 probe-exit=0 track=installed variant=qemu
ros2 lifecycle set /sensor_node activate --no-daemon --spin-time 3
ros2 lifecycle get /sensor_node --no-daemon --spin-time 3
```

```text probe-expect=2460 variant=qemu
Transitioning successful
active [3]
```

The talker's publisher opened as the node activated, and its next tick went
out. The first shell shows the listener again:

```text
I heard: reading …
```

The count goes on from wherever the talker's counter had reached: its
timer ran the whole time, and only the sending was held back. That is the difference
between a gated publisher and a stopped node.

## Deactivate it, and try a transition that is not allowed

```bash probe=2470 probe-run=120 probe-exit=0 track=installed variant=qemu
ros2 lifecycle set /sensor_node deactivate --no-daemon --spin-time 3
ros2 lifecycle get /sensor_node --no-daemon --spin-time 3
```

```text probe-expect=2470 variant=qemu
Transitioning successful
inactive [2]
```

The listener stops printing. Now ask for a transition that does not start
from `inactive`:

```bash probe=2480 probe-run=120 probe-exit=fail track=installed variant=qemu
ros2 lifecycle set /sensor_node deactivate --no-daemon --spin-time 3
```

```text probe-expect=2480 variant=qemu
Unknown transition requested
```

The machine refuses it and stays where it is, as stock ROS 2 does. To see
what it would accept from here:

```bash probe=2490 probe-run=120 probe-exit=0 track=installed variant=qemu
ros2 lifecycle list /sensor_node --no-daemon --spin-time 3
```

```text probe-expect=2490 variant=qemu
activate [3]
cleanup [2]
shutdown [6]
```

Activate it once more if you like: it sends again from the next tick, and
deactivating it stops it again, as often as you ask.

## Who drives a managed node

In this lab you drove the node by hand, from a shell. In a running system
something else does, and the node cannot tell the difference: every
`ros2 lifecycle set` is a call to the node's `change_state` service, with
the transition's id in the request. Whatever can call a ROS 2 service can
drive the node:

- **A supervisor node** on the host or on another board. It configures the
  nodes it is responsible for, checks what it must (a sensor answers, a
  limit switch is closed), activates them, and deactivates them when
  something goes wrong. Nav2's `lifecycle_manager` is a well-known example of
  such a node.
- **A test**, which wants the node to start at a known moment, and to stop
  again before the next case.
- **An operator**, with the commands you used.

The node's own image never drives it. That is the point of the lifecycle:
the decision to start work is taken outside the node, by whatever knows
whether the system is ready. A node that should simply work from boot needs
no lifecycle at all, and stays a plain `<node>`.

## Change it

Stop `nros run` with Ctrl-C. Two changes to try, one at a time:

- **Boot straight to work.** Set `autostart = "active"` in `system.toml`,
  or delete the `[lifecycle]` table, since `"active"` is the default. Run
  again: `ros2 lifecycle get /sensor_node` answers `active [3]` at once,
  and the listener hears from the first tick. The node is still managed, so
  a supervisor can still deactivate it.
- **Make the listener managed too.** Change `monitor_node`'s element to
  `<lifecycle_node>` as well. `ros2 lifecycle nodes` lists both, and each
  has its own state: activating one leaves the other where it was. Its
  subscription keeps working while it is `inactive`, because subscriptions
  are not gated. Only what it publishes would be.

`autostart` is one value for the whole image today: every managed node of
it boots to the same state. Give a node that should differ its transitions
after boot, with `ros2 lifecycle set` or a supervisor of your own.

## If it doesn't work

- **`ros2 lifecycle nodes` prints nothing.** The host shell has no
  `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp`, or `nros run` is not running. The
  router that `nros run` started is the only way the host reaches the
  board.
- **The talker publishes from boot.** The launch file still says `<node>`
  for it, or the `[lifecycle]` table is missing or says `"active"`. Rebuild
  happens on the next `nros run`; nothing else needs cleaning.
- **The build refuses the launch file.** Two managed nodes in one image ask
  for two `autostart` values in their contracts. Give the image one value.

## What just happened

- A launch file's `<lifecycle_node>` made one node managed, with no change
  to its code: the generated entry gave it the REP-2002 state machine and
  its five services, under its own name.
- `[lifecycle] autostart` chose where the image's managed nodes start.
- The node's publisher sent only while the node was `active`. Its timer,
  and the plain listener beside it, ran the whole time.
- The host drove the node with stock `ros2 lifecycle` commands, which got
  the same answers, and the same refusal, as from a stock ROS 2 node.
